claims.text: Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy evaluations are highly accurate but computationally expensive.
TOR-TILD is efficient for elemental and binary systems but slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems.
The proposed framework would actively refine a machine-learning potential using short ab initio molecular-dynamics trajectories at selected thermodynamic state points.
Training data would cover both solid and fluid phases.
The machine-learning potential would be integrated with an accelerated thermodynamic free-energy calculation resembling an improved TOR-TILD workflow.
The proposed model can encode vibrational dynamics, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
Active learning focused on configurations where critical physical effects occur will allow the model to reproduce the ab initio free-energy surface.
Extensive thermodynamic integration on the machine-learning surrogate can produce accurate solid and liquid phase free energies at lower computational cost.
The approach can reproduce free-energy landscapes for elemental and binary systems and eventually for multicomponent high-entropy systems.
The resulting phase free energies, melting temperatures, and fusion entropy changes will agree with explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics results within approximately 5% relative error.
The proposed method will be approximately 5–10 times faster than explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy workflows.
The proposed method will scale better than TOR-TILD for multicomponent high-entropy systems and avoid TOR-TILD's reported multicomponent slowdown.
Initial validation will use elemental and binary systems at temperatures ranging from below melting to high-temperature regimes.
The method will subsequently be applied to multicomponent high-entropy systems.
Performance is limited by whether the training data represent extreme anharmonicity and strong electron–vibration coupling.
Failure to sample rare but important configurations may cause systematic free-energy errors in high-entropy systems.
Systematic deviations greater than approximately 5% in phase free energies or derived melting and entropy observables relative to full ab initio molecular dynamics would falsify the hypothesis.
